source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS)
finding: 40 bespoke false-belief tasks. Each has a false-belief scenario, 3 true-belief controls, and reversed versions of all 4 (8 scenarios, 16 prompts). A model must pass all to score a task.
numbers: 11 LLMs. GPT-1, GPT-2, early GPT-3 models: 0%. davinci-002: 5% (CI 0-10). davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo: 20% (CI 11-29). ChatGPT-4 (June 2023): 75% (CI 66-84), compared with 6-year-old children (meta-analysis of 178 studies).
quote: ChatGPT-4 (from June 2023) solved 75% of the tasks, matching the performance of 6-y-old children
limits: Strict all-or-nothing scoring. Children comparison is a rough anchor from a different task set. ChatGPT-4 still failed at least one prompt in 25% of tasks.
agent_relevance: Scoring a social-belief probe only when matched controls also pass stops shortcut credit. Use paired controls in any check of our agent's other-mind reasoning.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS) - Unexpected Contents (Smarties) vs Unexpected Transfer (Maxi) split
finding: Unexpected Contents tasks were easier than Unexpected Transfer tasks for ChatGPT-4.
numbers: ChatGPT-4 solved 90% of Unexpected Contents tasks and 60% of Unexpected Transfer tasks (chi2=8.07, P=0.01). 20 tasks per type.
limits: Two task families only.
agent_relevance: Tracking a change of state across time is harder than reading a label. Expect state-update tracking to be a weak spot.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS) - effect of adding controls and revising items
finding: Earlier preprint versions scored higher. Reviewer-requested item edits and true-belief controls lowered scores, which shows how much shortcut credit the first version allowed.
numbers: davinci-003: 90% before updating items, 60% after updating, 20% after adding true-belief controls. ChatGPT-4: 95% before, 75% after both changes.
limits: ChatGPT-4 was more robust than davinci-003.
agent_relevance: Never trust a single-item pass on a social-reasoning probe. Pair every probe with a control that flips the answer.

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks (PNAS) - mechanism check with token probabilities
finding: The author tracked word probabilities as the story unfolded. Giving the protagonist access (informed protagonist, open container) moved predictions as a belief tracker would. He also notes false-belief tasks can sometimes be solved without ToM, by word order or frequency.
numbers: Unexpected Contents #19: P(popcorn) about 100% in the standard story and 88.5% to 99.7% across control variants. Transfer #19: P(John looks in basket) about 100% once John put the cat there and stayed there after Mark moved it.
limits: One worked story shown in depth. The author says he does not aim to settle whether this is true ToM.
agent_relevance: A token-probability probe can show whether an answer depends on who saw what. Cheap diagnostic for our scaffold.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Failed replication by variation. Small changes that keep ToM principles intact flipped GPT-3.5 answers. Example: a transparent bag where the protagonist can see the popcorn; the model still said Sam believes it holds chocolate.
numbers: Four variations on unexpected contents and two on unexpected transfer (transparent access, informed protagonist and similar). The model failed variations on tasks it passed in base form. Exact counts not recorded.
quote: the zero-hypothesis for model evaluation in intuitive psychology should be skeptical, and that outlying failure cases should outweigh average success rates
limits: Anecdotal outlier cases, one model (davinci-003-era GPT-3.5). Pi et al. 2024 (cited by Kosinski) suggest the model lacked a commonsense idea of transparency rather than ToM.
agent_relevance: Argues for a skeptical null: outlier failures outweigh average success. Test perceptual-access edits, not just the textbook story.

source: Sap, Le Bras, Fried, Choi (2022) Neural theory-of-mind? On the limits of social intelligence in large LMs
finding: GPT-3 is far below humans on social-commonsense and belief-tracking tasks. It does better on questions about the main agent than about others.
numbers: SocialIQa 55%, ToMi 60% (GPT-3-davinci). More than 30 points below humans on SocialIQa and more than 20 below fine-tuned models. Going from k=10 to k=35 shots added about 1 point.
quote: models struggle substantially at these Theory of Mind tasks, with well-below-human accuracies of 55% and 60% on SOCIALIQA and TOMI
limits: Pre-ChatGPT model. Later frontier models score much higher (Kosinski 2024, Strachan 2024).
agent_relevance: Baseline showing the gap was real in 2022. More shots did not fix it.

source: Sap et al. (2022) - pragmatics account of the limit
finding: The authors tie the failure to learning from text alone, with no grounded social interaction. davinci did better on agent-centric than other-focused questions.
numbers: Figures 3 and 4 in the paper; exact per-condition numbers not recorded.
limits: Theoretical argument, not a tested fix.
agent_relevance: Our agent also lacks a real second mind. Treat other-mind reasoning as a slot to check with code, not trust.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: a benchmark for stress-testing machine theory of mind in interactions
finding: Conversation benchmark with information asymmetry. Each fact is probed with six question types needing the same reasoning. Models pass the choice question but fail prerequisite questions (who could answer, who has access). The authors call such success illusory.
numbers: 13 LLMs. Models score more than 70 points below humans on average on the full set. GPT-4-0613 with CoT: 26.6 and 14.8 in two settings on the all-questions score (table rows read from PDF text; setting labels uncertain). 8.6% of question sets removed after crowd check.
quote: some instances of successful LLM ToM reasoning in FANTOM should be interpreted as illusory
limits: Human reference is graduate students on 32 sets. Fine-tuned Flan-T5 XL beat humans on single question types but not on the All metric.
agent_relevance: Consistency across several questions about the same mental fact is a strong test. Ask a belief question several ways and require agreement before trusting it.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM - chain of thought and fine-tuning
finding: Zero-shot chain of thought helped most models but did not close the gap. Fine-tuning gave above-human scores on single question types, not on the consistency metric.
numbers: CoT prompt 'let's think step by step' (Kojima). Gap to humans stays large on All.
limits: Benchmark not meant for training.
agent_relevance: Chain of thought alone does not fix other-mind tracking. Supports G1 and G3: need a check, not more words.

source: He et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: higher-order theory of mind benchmark
finding: As belief nesting order rises from 0 to 4, joint accuracy goes from near perfect to near zero. Deception lowers scores. Chain of thought gave no real gain.
numbers: 4 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-instant, Guanaco 65B). All under 60% standard accuracy. Deception and CoT: switching to CoT lowered accuracy on deceptive stories.
quote: As the ToM order increases from the zeroth to the fourth, the joint accuracy goes from near perfect to near zero.
limits: Only 4 models, 2023 versions. Order-4 stories are rare in real use.
agent_relevance: Beliefs about beliefs are hard past order 2. Do not rely on deep nesting; reduce to explicit who-knows-what tables.

source: Gu et al. (2026) SimpleToM: explicit vs applied theory of mind (ICLR 2026)
finding: Frontier models infer what a character knows but fail to use it to predict or judge behaviour. Explicit ToM does not transfer to applied ToM.
numbers: 21 models. Mental state above 95% for GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-405B, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4, GPT-5, o1, DeepSeek-R1. Behaviour prediction at least 30 points lower; o1-preview 84.1%; GPT-3.5 7.6%. Judgment 10% to 24.9% (below chance) for GPT-4o, Llama-405B, Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
quote: frontier LLMs may have the right conceptual knowledge/information about others' mental states when directly asked, they struggle to apply this knowledge
limits: Binary questions on constructed stories. Authors say near-perfect scores need explicit hints.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct match to our schema. Knowing a belief is not using it. Have the program inject the who-knows-what answer into the next step.

source: Gu et al. (2026) SimpleToM - interventions
finding: Reminding the model of its mental-state answer lifted behaviour prediction above 80%. A tailored chain-of-thought plus reminder gave near-perfect scores. Generic chain of thought did not.
numbers: With the reminder behaviour prediction above 80% for all, but behaviour judgment still 42.2% (GPT-4o) and 25.8% (Llama-3.1-405B). One GPT-4o item: 49.5% plain, 62.8% generic CoT, 87.4% custom CoT. Claude-3.5-Sonnet 97.1% average with reminder plus custom CoT.
limits: Hints are question-specific, so this is a ceiling, not a deployable gain. Authors: no simple test-time fix patched it reliably.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: feed the model its own checked intermediate result. A coded step asking 'is the actor aware?' then injecting the answer is worth testing.

source: Wang and Zhao (2024) Metacognitive prompting improves understanding in LLMs
finding: Five-stage prompt copying human metacognition: understand, preliminary judgment, critical evaluation, final decision with explanation, confidence. Beat chain of thought and plan-and-solve on language-understanding sets.
numbers: 4 LLMs (Llama-2-13b-chat, PaLM2-bison, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4), 10 datasets, zero-shot and 5-shot. On EUR-LEX gains of 15.0% to 26.9% over CoT. Gains over PS: 4.3% MedNLI, 9.6% UNFAIR-ToS, 12.4% EUR-LEX. Moderate gains on general NLU.
quote: I am 95% confident in my analysis.
limits: Verbalized confidence may be poorly calibrated (authors' own limit). Prompt is hand-built. Not about other minds or therapy.
agent_relevance: LLM use of metacognition by name, but its self-critique has no external signal, which G1 and G2 warn about. Weak single-source claim.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Battery of 5 tests (false belief, irony, faux pas, hinting, strange stories) given to GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA2-70B and 1,907 humans. GPT-4 matched or beat humans on most, not on faux pas.
numbers: 1,907 humans; per test N about 48 to 51. Models run repeatedly (n=15 observations). Faux pas: GPT-4 below humans (P=5.4e-5, r=0.55), GPT-3.5 near floor (r=0.72), LLaMA2-70B above humans (r=0.44). Hinting: GPT-4 above humans (P=0.040, r=0.32).
limits: Different human samples per test. Novel items added to guard against memorization.
agent_relevance: Mixed profile: do not treat ToM as one ability. Test each subskill.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) - faux pas follow-up
finding: GPT-4's faux pas failure is not lack of inference. Asked for likelihood ('more likely that they knew or did not know'), GPT-4 was perfect. Authors call it hyperconservative refusal to commit.
numbers: Faux pas likelihood test: GPT-4 100% correct. GPT-3.5 needed prompting in about 3% and failed about 9% of items. A belief-likelihood control with faux pas, neutral and knowledge-implied variants checked for bias toward 'did not know'.
quote: hyperconservative approach towards committing to conclusions rather than from a genuine failure of inference
limits: Explanation partly supported. Authors link it to inhibitory mitigation (safety tuning).
agent_relevance: Question wording changes whether the model reveals a belief it holds. Ask for ranked likelihoods, not yes-or-no commitments.

source: Frith (2012) The role of metacognition in human social interactions (Phil Trans R Soc B)
finding: Proposes that explicit metacognition lets people share confidence and make joint decisions. Describes a shift from implicit I-mode to shared we-mode. Group discussions are biased toward information members already share.
numbers: Reports the dyad task: group sensitivity beat the better partner. No new data.
quote: the ‘collective intelligence’ of human groups is higher when the group members have greater social sensitivity
limits: Theory review. Author leaves open whether implicit mentalizing deserves the name.
agent_relevance: Explicit sharing of confidence is the mechanism of group gain. An agent that reports calibrated confidence helps a group.

source: Bahrami et al. (2010) Optimally interacting minds (Science)
finding: Pairs did a two-interval contrast oddball task, first alone, then jointly by discussion. Pairs beat the better member. The weighted confidence sharing model (WCS) fit best.
numbers: Exp 1: 15 dyads; dyad sensitivity above better member t(14)=5.24, p<0.001. Coin flip rejected p<1e-5; behaviour-and-feedback rejected p<1e-3. Exp 2: equal noise t(10)=2.50 p=0.03; unequal noise no benefit t(21)=0.68 p=0.54; direct signal sharing rejected t(21)=4.52. Exp 4 (no feedback): benefit t(10)=2.68 p=0.022.
quote: For observers with very different sensitivities, two heads were worse than the better one.
limits: Read through the PMC page via WebFetch summary. Small samples (11 to 15 pairs). Simple perceptual task. Benefit lost when partners differ a lot.
agent_relevance: Founding result on confidence sharing. Gain depends on similar skill and honest confidence.

source: Bahrami et al. (2010) - rule for when pairing helps
finding: WCS predicts a benefit only if the weaker partner's sensitivity slope is at least about 0.41 of the stronger one's (sqrt 2 minus 1). Below that, a pair does worse than its best member.
numbers: Regression of collective benefit on relative sensitivity R2=0.51, slope 0.6+-0.09, intercept 0.74+-0.05 (WCS predicted 0.71). Most low-ratio dyads fell below break-even.
limits: Later work on calibration of confidence not opened here.
agent_relevance: Quantitative rule for ensembles of our own agents: a much weaker voter drags down a stronger one unless confidence is calibrated.

source: Normann and Morina (2018) The efficacy of metacognitive therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Front Psychol)
finding: MCT was far better than waitlist and moderately better than other therapies.
numbers: 25 studies, 15 randomized. Versus waitlist Hedges g=2.06 (CI 1.52-2.60, k=9). Versus cognitive and behavioural therapies g=0.69 at post-treatment (k=8) and g=0.37 at follow-up (k=7). GAD only post-treatment g=1.61 (CI 1.23-1.98, k=5).
limits: Risk of bias unclear or high in nearly a third of trials. One child trial. Waitlist effects are large by design.
agent_relevance: Clinical MCT changes how one relates to one's thoughts. Transfer to an LLM scaffold is indirect; keep as background.

source: Normann and Morina (2018) - allegiance check
finding: 13 trials had the MCT originator (Adrian Wells) as author. Their effects were larger than independent trials, but the gap shrank after removing an outlier.
numbers: Wells-group g=1.98 (CI 1.52-2.44) vs independent g=1.49 (CI 1.17-1.81), p=0.09. Without outlier Dammen 2015: g=1.84, k=12, p=0.19.
limits: Authors say allegiance bias may remain. Nordahl et al. 2018 is a balanced-author trial.
agent_relevance: Developer-run evaluations overstate gains. Matches our use of held-out checks.

source: Meta-analysis (2023) MCT versus CBT for generalized anxiety disorder (Cureus)
finding: Three RCTs only. MCT beat CBT on worry, anxiety and recovery.
numbers: PSWQ post-treatment mean difference -10.70 (CI -14.97 to -6.44); at 2 years -7.82 (CI -14.14 to -1.51). BAI post -8.83 (CI -14.57 to -3.08); 2 years -8.71. Recovery 67.36% MCT vs 42.86% CBT (RR 1.59, CI 1.19-2.11). I2=0%.
limits: Only 3 studies. Allegiance of authors not checked. Low-tier journal.
agent_relevance: Another sign MCT beats CBT, but on small samples.

source: Meta-analysis (2024) Metacognitive therapy in post-traumatic stress disorder
finding: Pre-post effect of MCT on PTSD symptoms was very large, from uncontrolled comparisons.
numbers: 7 studies, Hedges g=2.878 pre to post. Q statistic significant (studies differ). No publication bias detected. One study with children and teens (10-19).
limits: Uncontrolled pre-post effects are inflated compared with controlled ones (g=2.06 vs waitlist).
agent_relevance: Do not carry pre-post effect sizes into claims about our agent.

source: Nordahl and Wells (2018) Metacognitive therapy for social anxiety disorder: A-B replication series
finding: Metacognitive model of SAD: a perseverative thinking style (cognitive attentional syndrome, CAS) and the beliefs about thinking behind it. Three patients with different SAD subtypes each improved.
numbers: N=3; 8 sessions; gains largely kept at 6-month follow-up. Patient 3 no longer met criteria for major depression or avoidant personality disorder.
limits: Case series with no control for spontaneous recovery or non-specific factors. Authors call it preliminary.
agent_relevance: Social fear is kept alive by self-focused perseverative thinking. Agent lesson is limited.

source: Demetriou et al. (2020) Mapping mind-brain development: towards a comprehensive theory (J Intelligence)
finding: Mind has four systems: domain-specific, attention and working memory, reasoning, and cognizance (self-awareness). Four development cycles (episodic, realistic, rule-based, principle-based) emerge at birth, 2, 6 and 11 years. The AACog mechanism has three parts: alignment, abstraction, cognizance.
numbers: General factor g loads strongly on attention and memory, reasoning and cognizance markers. g shifts from executive to inferential to self-awareness processes with age.
quote: Awareness of mental processes is recycled with the changes in each cycle
limits: Review and theory. Brain claims are correlational. Concerns self-awareness, not beliefs about others' minds.
agent_relevance: Design idea: separate knowing what I process from processing. Weak link to our guardrails.

source: Trial protocol (2026) Transdiagnostic MCT vs disorder-specific CBT for anxiety disorders
finding: Pre-registered protocol (NCT06937892) for an 86-patient randomized trial in Stockholm. Notes only one adequately powered earlier transdiagnostic MCT vs CBT study (inpatient; d=0.70 favouring MCT).
numbers: Plan: N=86, GAD or SAD or PTSD, follow-up at 6 and 12 months, weekly mediator measures of metacognitions. About 50% remission after CBT, per the authors.
limits: No results yet. Independent replication is still thin.
agent_relevance: Open question of MCT superiority remains. Not strong evidence for us.

source: Wells and Matthews (1994, 1996) S-REF model of emotional disorder
finding: Self-regulatory executive function model: disorder is kept alive by a cognitive attentional syndrome (worry, rumination, threat monitoring, unhelpful coping) driven by beliefs about thinking. MCT trains detached mindfulness to drop the CAS.
numbers: Not opened this session. Description taken from the secondary papers read (Nordahl and Wells 2018, Normann and Morina 2018).
limits: Cited from secondary sources, not primary text.
agent_relevance: Core idea: control the process, not the content. Related to our doubt-on-signal rule.

source: Wells and Cartwright-Hatton (2004) A short form of the Metacognitions Questionnaire: MCQ-30
finding: Short self-report scale of metacognitive beliefs used across MCT work. Translations kept appearing in 2025 and 2026 (Turkish, Norwegian, Chinese adolescents, PTSD patients).
numbers: Not opened. About 672 citations in a Europe PMC listing.
limits: Only metadata seen. Psychometric details not recorded.
agent_relevance: None directly.

source: Frith (2012) - confidence vocabulary in dyads (from Bahrami line)
finding: Communicating confidence needs a shared scale. Bahrami pairs built a unique set of verbal descriptions during the experiment, and the optimum was reached only with free discussion.
numbers: Optimal pair performance appeared only when partners discussed before the joint decision.
limits: Review claim, not a new test.
agent_relevance: In multi-agent setups a shared calibrated confidence scale is a design element, not an extra.
